items.en: The Third Dhyāna: Its Five Factors and Their Varying Order
parent: The Third Dhyāna: Its Name and Cultivation

zh: 第二、明支義，開為二意：一、明支義；二、明前後不同。今明支者，三禪有五支。其五云何？一、捨；二、念；三、智；四、樂；五、一心。一、捨支者，得三禪樂定生時，捨喜心不悔，亦得言捨離三過；二、念支者，既得三禪之樂，念用三法守護，令樂增長；三、智支者，善巧三法離三過；四、樂支者，快樂樂遍身受；五、一心支者，受樂心息，一心寂定相貌，並如二禪發相中說。
en: Second, clarifying the meaning of the factors: this opens into two parts — clarifying the meaning of the factors; and clarifying their differing sequence across sources.

Here, clarifying the factors: the third dhyāna has five factors. What are these five? Equanimity; mindfulness; wisdom; happiness; and one-pointedness of mind. First, the factor of equanimity: upon attaining the third dhyāna, as the concentration of happiness arises, one relinquishes joy without any regret — this may also be spoken of as relinquishing the three faults already described. Second, the factor of mindfulness: having attained the third dhyāna's happiness, one uses mindfulness of the three methods to guard and protect it, allowing happiness to grow further. Third, the factor of wisdom: skillfully applying the three methods to leave the three faults behind. Fourth, the factor of happiness: immediate happiness, and happiness received throughout the whole body. Fifth, the factor of one-pointedness of mind: the mind of happiness having come to rest, the mind is one-pointed and still in its own mark — exactly as already described within the second dhyāna's own arising.

zh: 就此支中，約義自有四意：一者、三為方便支，二為證支。用念、慧、智三支調適樂定，令速得增長遍身，故說為方便支。受身樂、一心二支為證。此二一時發，是三禪之正主也。二者、四是自地立支。一望下地，立慧、念、樂，一心約自地立，捨支約捨下地喜不悔立也。三者、五支通得說作方便支。三如上說，下二何故亦得名方便邪？正言修樂增長，能感後樂故。一心亦爾，復望第六默然定體，五支例得名，因例得名方便。四者、五支通得說為證支。所證樂定時，自然生捨愛念樂定，如母護子，不由人勸，等智自發，籌量調適，五支俱皆屬證。問曰：若爾，前說並是方便，後說是證得，此意豈不碩相違反邪？答曰：並有其義，細尋自見。
en: Within these factors, there are, in terms of their sense, four further points to make.

First: three serve as expedient-means factors, and two serve as realization-factors. Using the three factors of mindfulness, discernment, and wisdom to regulate and adjust the concentration of happiness, causing it to grow and spread throughout the body all the more quickly, these are called expedient-means factors; receiving bodily happiness and one-pointedness of mind, these two factors, serve as the realization — these two arise together at one and the same time, and are the true, principal factors of the third dhyāna.

Second: four are established as factors with reference to this very stage itself, and one with reference to the stage below. Wisdom, mindfulness, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind are established with reference to this stage itself; the factor of equanimity is established with reference to relinquishing the lower stage's own joy without regret.

Third: all five factors may, in common, be called expedient-means factors. The first three are as already described above — why, then, can the remaining two also be named "expedient means"? Properly speaking, because the cultivation of happiness's own growth is able to bring about further happiness to come. One-pointedness of mind is exactly the same: looking further still toward the sixth, the substance of the concentration of silence, the five factors may, by the same pattern, all be named "expedient means" as its cause.

Fourth: all five factors may, in common, be called realization-factors. At the very moment this concentration of happiness is realized, equanimity arises naturally of itself, and one cherishes the concentration of happiness with mindful care, like a mother protecting her child, needing no urging from anyone else — equanimous wisdom arising spontaneously, deliberating and adjusting of its own accord; all five factors belong, in this sense, to realization. Question: if this is so, does this not directly contradict what was said just before — that some are expedient means and others are realization? Answer: both senses hold their own validity; examined closely, this can be seen for oneself.

zh: 第二、明支前後不同者，諸經及論各異。立次第，如《成實論》，明五支次第者：捨、念、智、受樂、一心。《阿毘曇》明次第：慧、念、樂、捨、一心。《大集》所出次第者：念、捨、慧、安、定。《纓絡經》中明次第：樂、護、念、智、一心。《釋論》明次第，文則不定，或與《成論》同，或與《纓絡》同。問曰：何獨此明支次第不定，餘禪不然邪？答曰：初禪等唯有一樂故，今三禪有二種樂故。由此二樂前後異故，中間迴互不定，是故諸經次第各立不同，而悉有意，必須得所以。
en: Second, clarifying the differing sequence of the factors: the various sūtras and treatises each differ in the sequence they establish. As the Satyasiddhi-śāstra clarifies the sequence of the five factors: equanimity, mindfulness, wisdom, received happiness, one-pointedness of mind. The Abhidharma clarifies the sequence as: wisdom, mindfulness, happiness, equanimity, one-pointedness of mind. The sequence given in the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra is: mindfulness, equanimity, wisdom, ease, concentration. The sequence clarified in the Yingluo Sūtra is: happiness, protection, mindfulness, wisdom, one-pointedness of mind. The sequence clarified in the Exegetical Treatise is not fixed, at times agreeing with the Satyasiddhi-śāstra, and at times agreeing with the Yingluo Sūtra.

Question: why is it only here that the sequence of the factors is unfixed, while it is not so for the other dhyānas? Answer: the first dhyāna and the others each have only a single kind of happiness; here, the third dhyāna has two kinds of happiness. Because these two kinds of happiness differ in their own before-and-after order, the sequence shifts back and forth without a single fixed order — hence the various sūtras each establish a differing sequence, though each carries its own sense, which must be properly grasped in turn.

zh: 第三、明體用。如《纓絡經》云：「五支為因，第六默然心為體。」第四、明淺深。五、明進退，並如前釋。第六、明功德者，具有離過、善心二德，如《大集經》說：「所言離者，謂離五蓋；具者，謂具五支。」據別，則但三禪獨有離喜過之德，餘義類上可知。
en: Third, clarifying substance and function: as the Yingluo Sūtra says, the five factors serve as the cause, and the sixth, the mind of silence, serves as the substance. Fourth, clarifying depth. Fifth, clarifying progress and regression: both follow the same pattern as already explained above. Sixth, clarifying merit: this is complete in both the merit of freedom from fault and the merit of a wholesome mind, as the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra says: "As for freedom: this means freedom from the five hindrances. As for completeness: this means completeness in the five factors." Discussed in its own particular sense, it is the third dhyāna alone that carries the distinct merit of freedom from the fault of joy; the remaining senses may be understood by the same pattern as above.

The treatise's explanation for why only the third dhyāna's factor-sequence varies across sources — because it alone has two distinct kinds of happiness whose relative ordering different texts weigh differently — is a good example of its general method: rather than treating textual disagreement as a problem to explain away, it treats the disagreement itself as evidence pointing to a genuine structural feature of the third dhyāna that the other three don't share. The fourfold analysis of the same five factors (three as means versus two as realization; four established with reference to this stage itself and one with reference to the stage below; all five as means toward what follows; all five as realization in their own right) is the treatise demonstrating that a single list can be sliced along several different valid axes at once — a caution against assuming any one of its own enumerations is the only correct way to see the material. This closes the whole of the third dhyāna.

items.en: The Fourth Dhyāna: Its Name, Cultivation, and Arising
items.zh: 四禪 · 釋名、明修習、明發相

zh:
次釋第四禪相，如經偈說：
聖人得能捨，餘人捨為難。
若能知樂患，見不動大安。
憂喜先已除，苦樂今亦斷，
捨念清淨心，入第四禪中。
第三禪中樂，無常動故苦，
欲界中斷憂，初二禪除苦。
是故佛世尊，第四禪中說，
先已斷憂苦，今則除苦樂。
今此四行偈，具明修證四禪之相。今釋第四禪，開為三意：一、釋名；二、明修習方法；三、明發相。
en:
Next, explaining the mark of the fourth dhyāna, as the sūtra verse says:
"The noble ones are able to relinquish it; for everyone else, relinquishing is difficult.
If one is able to see happiness as a trouble, one sees the great peace of the unmoving.
Sorrow and joy have already been removed; suffering and happiness are now cut off as well;
With equanimity and mindfulness, a pure mind, one enters the fourth dhyāna.
The happiness within the third dhyāna, being impermanent and unsettled, is itself suffering;
Sorrow was cut off within the desire realm; suffering was removed by the first and second dhyānas.
Hence the World-Honored Buddha, within the fourth dhyāna, says:
Sorrow and suffering have already been cut off; and now suffering and happiness are removed as well."
These four verse-lines (each of four phrases) clarify in full the marks of cultivating and realizing the fourth dhyāna. Here, explaining the fourth dhyāna, this opens into three parts: explaining the name; clarifying the method of cultivation; and clarifying the mark of its arising.

zh: 第一、釋四禪名者，禪名支林，四禪攬四支成定，於第四心中證得，故名四禪，猶是無覺無觀三昧聖默然攝，亦名不動定。《地持經》說：「名捨俱禪。」此定發時，體無苦樂，與微妙捨受俱發。此定與捨根相應，故名捨俱禪。
en: First, explaining the name of the fourth dhyāna: "dhyāna" means a grove of factors, and the fourth dhyāna gathers together four factors to form its own concentration, realized at this fourth stage of mind — hence it is named the fourth dhyāna. It, too, still belongs to the samādhi without initial thought or sustained reflection, the concentration of noble silence, and is also named the unmoving concentration. The Bodhisattva-bhūmi Sūtra calls it "the dhyāna joined with equanimity": when this concentration arises, its own substance is free of both suffering and happiness, arising together with the subtle and wondrous feeling of equanimity. This concentration corresponds with the equanimity-faculty — hence it is named the dhyāna joined with equanimity.

zh: 第二、明修習方法者，如上一行偈說，是樂「聖人得能捨，餘人捨為難。若能知樂患，見不動大安」。佛此偈具明修四禪方便。所以者何？行者欲得四禪，當應深見三禪過患。云何見過？初欲得樂，一心勤求，大為辛苦，既得守護愛著，是亦為苦。一旦失壞，則復受苦，是故經說：「第三禪中樂，無常動故苦。」又此樂法覆念，令不清淨，行者既深見三禪樂有大苦之患，應一心厭離，求四禪種不動定，爾時於三禪邊地當修六行方法，例如前說，亦應用於三法除遣：一、不著；二、訶責；三、觀析。行此三法，即三禪謝滅，而四禪未到中間，必有定前發，與觀相應等相貌，並如上說，不同憂、喜。過如前說。
en: Second, clarifying the method of cultivation: as the first verse-line (of four phrases) given above says, this happiness is such that "the noble ones are able to relinquish it; for everyone else, relinquishing is difficult. If one is able to see happiness as a trouble, one sees the great peace of the unmoving." The Buddha, within this verse, clarifies in full the expedient means for cultivating the fourth dhyāna. Why is this? The practitioner wishing to attain the fourth dhyāna should deeply perceive the trouble present within the third dhyāna.

How does one perceive this trouble? At first, wishing to attain happiness, one seeks it single-mindedly, with great toil and hardship; and, having attained it, guarding and cherishing it with attachment, this too is a form of suffering; and, should it ever be lost or broken, one suffers all over again from this as well — hence the sūtra says: "The happiness within the third dhyāna, being impermanent and unsettled, is itself suffering." Furthermore, this dharma of happiness clouds over mindfulness, keeping it from being pure. The practitioner, having deeply perceived that the third dhyāna's happiness carries within it this great trouble of suffering, should single-mindedly grow weary of it and turn away, seeking instead the fourth dhyāna's own seed of unmoving concentration. At this point, at the border of the third dhyāna, one should cultivate the method of the six practices, following the same pattern as already described, and should likewise apply the same three methods to dispel it: non-attachment; reproach; and analytic contemplation. Practicing these three methods, the third dhyāna thereby passes away and is extinguished; and, with the fourth dhyāna not yet reached, in the interval between them, a preliminary concentration necessarily arises, corresponding with contemplation, in the same manner as already described above — differing only in no longer involving sorrow or joy. Its own fault is as already described above as well.

zh: 第三、釋四禪發相，此如上三行偈說證，例前開為六意：一、正明證四禪；二、明支義；三、明體用；四、明淺深；五、明進退；六、明功德。第一、明四禪發相。行者因中間禪修行不止，得入未到地，心無動散，即四禪方便定。於後其心豁然開發，定心安隱，出入息斷，定發之時，與捨俱生，無苦無樂，空明寂靜，善法眷屬類如前說，但無事用喜樂動轉之異。爾時心如明鏡不動，亦如淨水無波，絕諸亂想，正念堅固，猶如虛空，是名世間真實禪定，無諸垢染。
en: Third, explaining the mark of the fourth dhyāna's own arising: this is realized exactly as the three remaining verse-lines given above describe, and, following the same pattern as before, opens into six parts — directly clarifying the realization of the fourth dhyāna; clarifying the meaning of its factors; clarifying its substance and function; clarifying its depth; clarifying its progress and regression; and clarifying its merits.

First, clarifying the mark of the fourth dhyāna's own arising: the practitioner, through the intermediate dhyāna's own unceasing practice, comes to enter the "not-yet-arrived" state, the mind free of agitation or scattering — this is precisely the fourth dhyāna's own preliminary concentration. Afterward, the mind opens out and is brought forth, the concentrated mind at peace, the in-breath and out-breath both cut off; at the very moment concentration arises, it arises together with equanimity, free of both suffering and happiness, empty, luminous, and still, its wholesome dharma and retinue following the same pattern already described — differing only in having no excited stirring of joy or happiness present at all. At that point, the mind is like a bright mirror, unmoving, and like clear water free of any ripple, every scattered thought cut off entirely, right mindfulness firm and secure, just like empty space itself — this is named the true, genuine dhyāna-concentration of the mundane world, free of any defiling stain whatsoever.

zh: 行者住是定中，心不依善，亦不附惡，無所依倚，無形無質，亦無若干種種色相，而內成就淨色之法。何以得知？若無淨色根本，則不應於定中對因緣時，發種種色，如通四無量心、勝處、一切處變化等色，並依四禪。若以不見諸色謂言無色者，應如虛空處定三種色滅，一切色法悉不得現。今一切色法自在得現，而於定法無所損減者，當知是真色定。譬如明鏡，體是淨色，故隨對諸色，一切得現；若無淨色為本者，終不於虛空中現諸色像。復次，此四禪種智定一心故，念常清淨，亦名不動定，亦名不動智慧。於此禪中，若欲轉緣學一切事，隨意成就，一切神通變化，霔雨說法，莫不從此定出。如經說：「佛於四禪為根本。」
en: The practitioner, abiding within this concentration, the mind no longer relies on the wholesome, nor clings to the unwholesome, with nothing at all to depend upon or lean against — without shape, without substance, and without any particular kind of form or mark whatsoever — and yet, within, accomplishes the dharma of pure form. How is this known? Were there no root of pure form present at all, then, within concentration, in response to the proper causes and conditions, it ought not be possible for various forms to be brought forth at all — as with the forms of the supernormal powers, the four immeasurable minds, the stations of mastery, the totality-bases, transformations, and the like, all of which depend upon the fourth dhyāna. If one were to conclude, simply because no forms are seen, that there is therefore no form present at all, then, as in the concentration of the sphere of boundless space, where the three kinds of form are extinguished, no form-dharma whatsoever ought to be capable of manifesting there either. Here, however, every form-dharma is able to manifest freely, with no diminishment at all to the dharma of concentration itself — hence one should know that this is a concentration of true form. It is like a bright mirror: its own substance is pure form, and so, whatever is placed before it, every form is able to appear within it; were there no pure form as its basis, it could never manifest any image of form within empty space at all.

Furthermore: because this fourth dhyāna's own wise concentration is one-pointed in mind, mindfulness is forever pure — hence it is also named the unmoving concentration, and also named unmoving wisdom. Within this dhyāna, should one wish to shift one's object and study any matter whatsoever, it is accomplished exactly as intended — every supernormal power and transformation, the raining down of rain and the teaching of the Dharma — all issue from this very concentration without exception. As the sūtra says: "The Buddha takes the fourth dhyāna as his own root and foundation."

The fourth dhyāna's "true form" argument is a genuinely careful piece of reasoning against a natural misreading: a concentration with "no shape, no substance, no particular mark" might seem to be a formless attainment, indistinguishable from the boundless-space sphere that actually does extinguish form — but the treatise's test is functional rather than descriptive. If the fourth dhyāna can still give rise to visible transformations (as the basis for the four immeasurable minds, the stations of mastery, and the totality-bases' own display of forms), it must retain "pure form" as its own hidden root, the way a mirror's own clarity — itself colorless — is precisely what allows any color to appear in it. This is the treatise's own criterion for distinguishing dhyāna from formlessness by what it can still do, not by what it superficially resembles.

quiz.q: What are the third dhyāna's five factors?
quiz.why: "The third dhyāna has five factors. What are these five? Equanimity; mindfulness; wisdom; happiness; and one-pointedness of mind."

quiz.q: In the first sense, which of the third dhyāna's factors are expedient-means factors and which are realization factors?
options: three are expedient means (regulating happiness to grow); bodily happiness and one-pointedness are realization, the true principal factors
quiz.why: "Three serve as expedient-means factors, and two serve as realization-factors ... receiving bodily happiness and one-pointedness of mind, these two factors, serve as the realization — these two arise together at one and the same time, and are the true, principal factors of the third dhyāna."

quiz.q: Why, according to the text, is only the third dhyāna's factor sequence unfixed across sources?
options: the other dhyānas have one kind of happiness; the third has two, whose order differs, so the sequence shifts
quiz.why: "The first dhyāna and the others each have only a single kind of happiness; here, the third dhyāna has two kinds of happiness. Because these two kinds of happiness differ in their own before-and-after order, the sequence shifts back and forth without a single fixed order."

quiz.q: What else is the fourth dhyāna called, and what does the Bodhisattva-bhūmi call it?
options: the unmoving concentration; the dhyāna joined with equanimity, free of suffering and happiness, arising with subtle equanimity
quiz.why: "It ... is also named the unmoving concentration. The Bodhisattva-bhūmi Sūtra calls it 'the dhyāna joined with equanimity': when this concentration arises, its own substance is free of both suffering and happiness, arising together with the subtle and wondrous feeling of equanimity."

quiz.q: How does the practitioner see the trouble in the third dhyāna's happiness?
options: seeking it is toil, guarding it with attachment is suffering, losing it is suffering again; and happiness clouds mindfulness
quiz.why: "At first, wishing to attain happiness, one seeks it single-mindedly, with great toil and hardship; and, having attained it, guarding and cherishing it with attachment, this too is a form of suffering; and, should it ever be lost or broken, one suffers all over again from this as well ... Furthermore, this dharma of happiness clouds over mindfulness."

quiz.q: What marks the arising of the fourth dhyāna, and what similes are used?
options: the breath ceases, it arises with equanimity, free of suffering and happiness; the mind like a still mirror, like water without ripples
quiz.why: "The concentrated mind at peace, the in-breath and out-breath both cut off; at the very moment concentration arises, it arises together with equanimity, free of both suffering and happiness ... At that point, the mind is like a bright mirror, unmoving, and like clear water free of any ripple."

quiz.q: How does the text show that the fourth dhyāna inwardly accomplishes "pure form"?
options: transformative forms appear through it, which would be impossible without pure form, as in boundless space where form is extinguished; like a mirror whose pure substance reflects every image
quiz.why: "Were there no root of pure form present at all, then, within concentration ... it ought not be possible for various forms to be brought forth at all ... It is like a bright mirror: its own substance is pure form, and so, whatever is placed before it, every form is able to appear within it."

quiz.q: The text quotes "The Buddha takes the fourth dhyāna as his root." What does this show?
options: within it, whatever one turns to is accomplished; every power, transformation, and teaching issues from it
quiz.why: "Within this dhyāna, should one wish to shift one's object and study any matter whatsoever, it is accomplished exactly as intended — every supernormal power and transformation ... all issue from this very concentration without exception. As the sūtra says: 'The Buddha takes the fourth dhyāna as his own root and foundation.'"
